meta.titre: Chemical bonding: ionic, covalent and metallic, with giant structures

sections.contenu_markdown: Table salt from the coast, the graphite in a pencil, the copper wire in a house in Yaoundé and the water you drink are all held together by chemical bonds. The type of bond decides whether a substance melts easily, conducts electricity or dissolves in water. Diamond cuts through the rock when a borehole is drilled, while the graphite in the same family of carbon is soft enough to write with. The GCE O/L paper asks you to name the type of bond, to draw dot and cross diagrams, to write formulae, and to explain properties such as melting point and conductivity.

items: A metal atom has few electrons in its outer shell, and a non-metal atom has more.
Atoms with a full outer shell, such as the noble gases, are stable and unreactive.
An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons.
A molecule is a group of atoms joined together.

sections.titre: Chemical bonding: ionic, covalent and metallic
sections.contenu_markdown:
Atoms bond to obtain a **full outer shell**, like a noble gas.

**Ionic bond.** Electrons are **transferred** from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. The atoms become oppositely charged ions, which attract each other strongly and form a giant lattice. Example: sodium (2,8,1) gives one electron to chlorine (2,8,7), forming $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ (2,8) and $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ (2,8,8).

**Covalent bond.** A pair of electrons is **shared** between two non-metal atoms. Each atom has a full outer shell by counting the shared pair. Examples: $\mathrm{H_2}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$. Oxygen has a **double** bond and nitrogen has a **triple** bond.

**Metallic bond.** Positive metal ions sit in a "sea" of free (delocalised) electrons, which hold the ions together.

| Property | Ionic compound | Simple covalent compound | Metal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Melting and boiling point | High (strong attractions between ions) | Low (weak forces between molecules) | Usually high |
| Conducts as a solid | No | No | Yes |
| Conducts when molten or dissolved | Yes (ions move) | No | Yes (when molten) |
| Dissolves in water | Many do | Many do not | No |

**Dot and cross diagram.** Draw only the outer shell of each atom. Use dots for the electrons of one atom and crosses for the electrons of the other. For ionic bonding, show the transfer, put each ion in brackets and write its charge. For covalent bonding, show the shared pair where the shells overlap.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the formula of an ionic compound is asked
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Write the ions and balance the charges so the total is zero (swap the numbers of the charges).

| Group I | Group II | Group III | Group VI | Group VII |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$, $\mathrm{K^{+}}$ | $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ | $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ | $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$ | $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ |

Common compound ions: $\mathrm{OH^{-}}$, $\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}$, $\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}$.

Examples: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ give $\mathrm{MgO}$. $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ give $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$, because $2 \times 3 = 3 \times 2 = 6$ charges of each sign. $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}$ give $\mathrm{Ca(NO_{3})_{2}}$, using brackets when a compound ion is repeated. A Group I metal gives a chloride of the type MCl, for example $\mathrm{NaCl}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a dot and cross diagram of a molecule is asked
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Molecule | Shared pairs | Lone pairs on the central atom |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ | 1 single bond | none |
| $\mathrm{HCl}$ | 1 | 3 on Cl |
| $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ | 2 | 2 on O |
| $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$ | 3 | 1 on N |
| $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$ | 4 | none |
| $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ | 2 double bonds | 2 on each O |
| $\mathrm{N_{2}}$ | 1 triple bond | 1 on each N |

Each atom (except hydrogen) ends with **8 electrons** in its outer shell, counting shared pairs. Hydrogen ends with 2.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When diamond, graphite or the properties of a solid are asked
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Allotropy** is the existence of an element in two or more different forms in the same physical state, with different arrangements of atoms. Carbon has the allotropes **diamond** and **graphite**.

| | Diamond | Graphite |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Each carbon bonded to 4 others in a giant lattice | Each carbon bonded to 3 others, in layers |
| Hardness | Hardest natural substance | Soft, layers slide over each other |
| Electrical conduction | No (no free electrons) | Yes (one free electron per atom) |
| Uses | Cutting and drilling tools, jewellery | Pencil leads, lubricants, electrodes |

sections.enonce_markdown: Describe, using outer-shell electrons only, how magnesium and oxygen bond to form magnesium oxide, and state three properties of the compound. (Magnesium is atomic number 12 and oxygen is 8.)

etapes.justification: The outer shell tells how many electrons are lost or gained.

etapes.action: Show the loss of electrons by magnesium.
etapes.justification: A metal atom loses its 2 outer electrons to reach a full shell.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Mg loses 2 electrons and becomes $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, **2,8**, shown in brackets with the charge 2+

etapes.action: Show the gain of electrons by oxygen.
etapes.justification: A non-metal atom with 6 outer electrons gains 2 to reach 8.
etapes.resultat_markdown: O gains the 2 electrons and becomes $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$, **2,8**, shown in brackets with 8 outer electrons and the charge $2-$

etapes.action: Explain the bond and the formula.
etapes.justification: The two ions have equal and opposite charges, so they combine one to one.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The strong electrostatic attraction between $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ is the **ionic bond**. The formula is $\mathrm{MgO}$.

etapes.justification: Ions are held in a giant lattice by strong forces.
etapes.resultat_markdown: **High melting point**, **does not conduct** as a solid, and **conducts when molten**.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Magnesium oxide, $\mathrm{MgO}$, forms by **transfer of 2 electrons** from magnesium to oxygen, giving an ionic lattice of $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$.

items.erreur_markdown: In ionic bonding, the atoms share electrons.
items.pourquoi_faux: Sharing is covalent bonding. In ionic bonding electrons move completely from one atom to the other.
items.correction_markdown: Ionic: **transfer** of electrons. Covalent: **sharing** of a pair.

items.erreur_markdown: Solid sodium chloride conducts electricity because it contains ions.
items.pourquoi_faux: In the solid the ions are fixed in position and cannot move.
items.correction_markdown: It conducts only when **molten or dissolved**, when the ions are free to move.

items.erreur_markdown: Simple covalent compounds have low melting points because the covalent bonds are weak.
items.pourquoi_faux: The covalent bonds inside each molecule are strong. Only the forces between molecules are weak, and these are overcome when the compound melts.
items.correction_markdown: Low melting point is due to **weak forces between molecules**.

items.erreur_markdown: Diamond and graphite are both made of carbon, so both conduct electricity.
items.pourquoi_faux: In graphite each atom has a free electron, but in diamond all four outer electrons are in bonds.

items.erreur_markdown: The formula of aluminium oxide is $\mathrm{Al_3O_2}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The subscripts were taken from the wrong place. The aluminium ion is $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and the oxide ion is $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$, so charges must balance.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the type of bonding (ionic, covalent or metallic) in each of: sodium chloride, carbon dioxide, copper, methane, potassium bromide.
items.solution_markdown: Sodium chloride: **ionic**. Carbon dioxide: **covalent**. Copper: **metallic**. Methane: **covalent**. Potassium bromide: **ionic**.

items.enonce_markdown: Write the formulae of (a) magnesium chloride, (b) aluminium oxide, (c) calcium nitrate, (d) ammonium sulphate. ($A_r$: Ca = 40; N = 14; O = 16; H = 1; S = 32.) (e) Calculate the relative formula mass of calcium nitrate.

(a) Describe the bonding in ammonia, $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$, using outer-shell electrons only. (b) Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point and conducts when molten, while methane has a low melting point and never conducts. (c) Explain why graphite is used for the electrodes in electrolysis but diamond is not.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Nitrogen (2,5) shares one pair of electrons with each of 3 hydrogen atoms. There are **3 shared pairs** and **1 lone pair** on nitrogen, giving nitrogen 8 outer electrons and each hydrogen 2. (b) Sodium chloride is a giant lattice of ions with strong electrostatic attractions, so a lot of energy is needed to melt it. When molten, the ions are free to move and carry charge. Methane is made of separate molecules with weak forces between them, and it has no ions or free electrons, so it never conducts. (c) Graphite has **free electrons** that carry current, and it is unreactive and withstands heat. Diamond has no free electrons.

items_markdown: **Ionic**: metal to non-metal, electrons **transferred**, giant lattice of ions, conducts only when molten or dissolved.
**Covalent**: non-metals **share** pairs of electrons; simple molecules have low melting points and do not conduct.
**Metallic**: positive ions in a sea of free electrons, so metals conduct and are malleable.
Balance the charges to write formulae: $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$, $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$, $\mathrm{Ca(NO_{3})_{2}}$.
Allotropes are different forms of the same element: diamond is hard and does not conduct; graphite is soft and conducts.
